Name: Claire Jordan
Question: Is anyone familiar with the "Cosmological Argument"? It says that everything that has existed has had a cause, and people have used this to argue that God should exist. What is wrong with this idea?
Answer: What’s wrong with it is that is doesn’t solve anything. What caused God? If God doesn’t need a cause, why does the universe need a cause? It’s just giving a new label to the same problem.

Name: Claire Jordan
Question: What do you think would have been the "best alternative" or the least damaging alternative for Alan Turing after his 1952 trial which was a dead end: prison or the harmful chemical castration he eventually underwent?
Answer: I know this isn’t a direct answer, but please note that the medical evidence indicates that Turing died by accident, as a result of sloppy lab safety. The idea that he committed suicide was invented by a coroner who just assumed that all gay men must be fragile hysterics. The chemical castration ended a long time before his death, and he seems to have regarded it as a bit of a joke: he was significantly autistic and didn’t give a flying fuck what anybody outside his own immediate circle thought of him. The people who scream about his being hounded to suicide, so that they can milk his death for melodramatic outrage, are perpetuating what was only ever a homophobic slur against him. But in the unlikely event that he *did* commit suicide, his friends reported that what was preying on his mind at the time of his death was the fact that he had just had a very bad reading from a fairground psychic. In answer to the question, it’s difficult to know what else the police could have done. Having consensual sex with a 19-year-old soldier *shouldn’t* have been illegal, but it was (and iirc was viewed as paedophilia since the soldier was under 21 which, again, is ridiculous since at 19 a soldier was allowed to take part in actual battle). And Turing had so little awareness of social norms that he happily told the police all about his favourite sexual positions. If he had been even mildly discreet they would probably have found an excuse to let him go, but his total lack of conversational filters didn’t leave them with many options.

Name: Claire Jordan
Question: Can you still love an author's work even if in real life that author is transphobic?
Answer: It’s an interesting question: just how bad a person does an artist have to be before we stop enjoying their work? I dislike Jo Rowling - and I did even before she metamorphosed into Umbridge - but I still like the characters she created. I love the Beatles, even though Lennon was a violent bully. Steinbeck was said to be a horrible person in real life, but we admire his writing. We still admire the beautiful sculptures of Eric Gill, and nobody is calling for their removal, even though he was an all-purpose pervert who had sex not only with his children but with his dog. We still revere Charlie Chaplin, even though he was a bit of a hebephile even by the standards of the 1930s. We even admire the films of Leni Riefenstahl even though some of them were produced for the Nazis. We can still appreciate the artistry while rejecting the message. But the band LostProphets went into free-fall when it was revealed that their lead singer’s hobby was raping infants, and I don’t think I could separate the crime from the performance. Part of it is that with a singer you have to interact with the actual performer, whereas a book or a sculpture is at a remove from the person who created them. But that ought to apply to Lennon and Chaplin too - so what makes the difference?

Question: Does clothing actually have a gender? If normal is defined differently by different people then why are gender norms for clothing pushed so much? Why are men so afraid to show any femininity clothing or otherwise?
Answer: The *cut* of clothing has a gender, because men and women tend to be a different shape. Women can usually get away with male shirts just by wearing them several sizes too big, but a man in a woman’s shirt is likely to end up with two sad little empty flaps on the chest. Grayson Perry manages to look good in a frock because he can afford to have his tailored to fit. Note the high waist and big collar, which distract attention away from the lack of a bust.
